## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#one-number-the-whole-class}

<!-- The last fragment differs by format: the slide decks that teach the
     specification menu (deck: {menu: true} in their YAML) name it, the others
     list the choices. -->

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Everyone with the same analyst gets the same value, to the third decimal, and every recorded value comes back. That is reproducibility, and it is the easy R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You all ran the *same code*. The five analysts of the robustness study each wrote their own, on the same public file, and came back with five different numbers and two different verdicts.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of them was careless. They made different choices[, and the options that they chose from make up the **menu**]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.menu"}[ about **which names** to compare, **which emails** to count and **which test** to run]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}.
:::
::::

::: notes
Different people, on different machines, reproduced different analysts, and everyone with the same analyst landed on the same number, matching the record to the third decimal. That is reproducibility, and it came cheaply, because you ran code written for the workshop on a file that anyone can download. [advance] The five analysts themselves had the same public file, each wrote their own analysis, and they came back with five different numbers and two different verdicts on whether the data supported the claim. [advance] None of them was careless. Four of the five published their scripts on the OSF, and in my reading these are competent pieces of work, so the spread arguably comes from the choices that each analyst made rather than from the quality of the work.
:::
